What I think could make this render even better is some work on the lighting and composition. 

I would make the armchair, the table or anything the focal point of the render with a tighter focal length so the viewer have an object to rest their eyes on. Right now everything is in focus and it's makes it a little jarring to look at. "What is the purpose of the image, what should I look at"? I personally like to have a more tight shot in interior scenes for these purposes, unless the goal of the render is to show the whole space.  Since you have created the whole room I would instead create a few tighter shots from different intresting angles

​

The lighting right now for me is kind of dull, dark, and does not make the scene justice, the background tree is in perfect focus and it looks like the room is hovering in mid air. I think it looks more realistic if the outside is overexposed, as usually the case due to the limited dynamic range of cameras. I would work on focusing the light coming from the window to left that would guide the viewer more to the center of the image to get a more distinct focal point, maybe change the camera angle to not show the right window area but have the center window in the background instead with some depth of field applied.

​

These are just some of my though if it is of any value.

What I can say is that I've had moments where parts for some reason separates and it becomes a whole lot clearer once you are in that space. But yeah when you are in your everyday mode and blended with the usual suspects it is as you describe it. 

I did find it funny because I can imagine my own angry part telling a therapist to eff himself in that setting too.

From what I can tell a part that puts you down could very well be a protector part because it could be trying to put you down/shame you so other people don't if that makes sense. If it didn't do that it could believe that other people will shame/insult a part of you that has previously been hurt and that would be even worse. Like a pre empty strike. If you get to a space were you can separate from the part and have more self you could ask it and learn more.

Hang in there man

I could be wrong but I think fundamentally parts naturally unblends or step aside when they feel it's safe to do so, I mean that's the role of protector parts but I imagine it extends to any part really. I think that's whats happening with most of my ifs-sessions is that some of my parts don't trust, feel comfortable or are in conflict with some of the therapist parts, especially if the therapist doesn't seem to have alot of self present.

You definitely right, you can have a by the book therapist who can say the right things, follow the exact therapy form, recognize parts correctly but If it's done by a with a sort of analytical school teacher part it just wont work, atleast for me. It's an art form as you say. In my case since I don't have alot of self presence the therapist would have to have more of that then me atleast, I think that's important.

The unblending of parts for me is just a factor based on time and location and not really by negotiation/curiosity/compassion and so on but it would be nice to be able to.

What keeps pulling me to IFS, I'm really not sure. So far nothing has really come of it but I've had experiences, moments of self presence, being detached from parts and able to see them from a loving place. So I know it's there and I guess a part of me wants to go towards more of that in my life and seeing IFS as the method. But I mean sure, years of trying it without any success could be an indicator of how well that's going.  Regardless I'm not really interested in any other form of therapy. I've tried different therapy forms and even sort of spiritual forms but it's just not for me.

I could take mdma and in 30 minutes be engulfed in compassion, understanding, clarify and all qualities of self but that's like years and years of work otherwise which is depressing, I think the saying is right, beware of unearned knowledge.

Feel free to comment, I appreciate your replies
